analysis.one_liner: Forces private equity and for-profit health care companies to disclose finances, get licenses, and give notice before closing hospitals.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 14 House Democrats and no Republicans, was sent to four House committees and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets private equity firms, real estate investment trusts, and other for-profit corporations that own hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, doctor practices, and other health care businesses. It would require them to report detailed financial and staffing information publicly, require private equity firms to obtain a federal license to buy health care providers, let the Health Secretary block or delay risky deals, require 90 days' notice and a public review before hospitals close or cut essential services, and move pension debts to the front of the line in bankruptcies. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities served by private-equity-owned or for-profit hospitals and nursing homes, who would get public data on who owns their facilities and warnings before closures; health care workers, whose pension claims would take priority in bankruptcy and whose wages, staffing, and working conditions would be tracked; and communities that would get a formal chance to comment before a hospital shuts down or drops essential services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and local communities

how_it_helps.text: Private equity funds that control health care companies would have to report debts, fees extracted from providers, dividends, executive pay, staffing levels, closures, and complaints about wage and worker-safety violations, with the data made public [S2].

Private equity firms would need a federal license to buy or invest in health care entities, and the Secretary could deny or revoke it and force divestment for price gouging, understaffing, or blocking access to care [S2].

Hospitals would have to give 90 days' notice before closing or discontinuing services, submit a plan to preserve access to essential services, and take part in a public comment process, with the Secretary able to work out an alternative plan to keep essential services running [S2].
Health care businesses with pension withdrawal liability would pay that debt first in bankruptcy, ahead of other creditors, protecting workers' pensions when a facility collapses [S2].

The bill would study and could temporarily bar private equity purchases of health care companies while a task force reviews price gouging, understaffing, and access barriers, and research the impact of eventually banning for-profit ownership of health care altogether [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, real estate investment trusts that lease hospital buildings back to operators, and for-profit health care corporations, which would face disclosure costs, license fees, possible escrow and capital-investment requirements, penalties, and deals the government could block. Compliance costs could ultimately show up in returns to those funds' investors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity, REITs, and for-profit operators

drawbacks.text: The reporting demands are sweeping — up to 38 categories of financial, political, and staffing data from equity-owned firms and 24 from other for-profit firms — and even with a directive to reduce duplication, compliance costs would be substantial and fall on covered firms and ultimately their investors [S2].

The bill gives the Health Secretary broad discretion — to define 'essential services,' review sale-leaseback terms, issue or revoke private equity licenses, and bar purchases pending task force study — which critics of such regulatory schemes argue could slow legitimate investment in struggling rural hospitals and delay needed closures [S2].

The bill does not ban private equity or for-profit ownership of health care now; it researches that step, so private-equity-owned hospitals and nursing homes would continue operating under disclosure and licensing rules rather than an outright prohibition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and workers, the benefits are concrete: transparency about who owns their hospitals, pension protection in bankruptcy, and a public process before closures. The costs are concentrated on the industries being regulated and include real compliance burdens and the risk that licensing and review requirements deter investment in facilities that need it. The bill's heaviest tools are conditional and discretionary, so its practical bite would depend heavily on how future administrations enforced it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees when introduced in July 2024, then referred to a Health subcommittee in December, and neither any committee nor the House ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Health Over Wealth Act on July 25, 2024, with 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1][S3].

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — a split referral that requires multiple committees to act before a bill can advance [S4].

Nearly five months later, on December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, a step that keeps a bill within a committee rather than moving it toward the floor [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds, real estate investment trusts, and for-profit health care companies are better off: none of the disclosure, licensing, closure-notice, or bankruptcy-priority requirements took effect, so they face no new oversight of their health care holdings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and for-profit health care owners

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship, which was entirely Democratic.

industries.industry: Private equity firms investing in health care
industries.note: The bill would force funds that control hospitals, nursing homes, and doctor practices to publicly disclose their debt levels, fees extracted from providers, dividends, and political spending, and would require them to obtain a federal license that can be revoked for understaffing or price gouging. It could also bar new health care purchases while a task force studies the sector [S2].

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill would ban sale-leaseback deals whose terms weaken a health care provider's finances or put public health at risk, and would stop treating rents from health care property as qualifying REIT income for tax purposes, removing a tax advantage [S2].

industries.industry: For-profit hospital, nursing home, and physician-practice operators
industries.note: All for-profit firms owning health care providers would face extensive public financial reporting, staffing and wage disclosures, worker-complaint reporting, and 90-day notice plus public review before closing a hospital or dropping essential services [S2].

industries.industry: Community health centers, teaching health centers, and safety-net hospitals
industries.note: License application fees and civil penalties collected from private equity firms would flow to the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving low-income patients [S2].

industries.industry: Financial institutions lending to health care buyouts
industries.note: Lenders to heavily indebted health care takeovers would face public disclosure of their loans and, in bankruptcy, lower priority than workers' pension withdrawal liability claims [S2].
